claim: Reduced copy number of ribosomal protein (Rp) genes adversely affects both flies and mammals.
source: Reduced copy number of ribosomal protein (Rp) genes adversely affects both flies and mammals.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract summarizing known effects of Rp gene mutations across species.

claim: Xrp1 encodes a reportedly Drosophila-specific AT-hook, bZIP protein responsible for many of the effects including the elimination of Rp mutant cells by competition with wild type cells.
source: Xrp1 encodes a reportedly Drosophila-specific AT-hook, bZIP protein responsible for many of the effects including the elimination of Rp mutant cells by competition with wild type cells.
evidence: This statement cites prior knowledge about Xrp1's role and characteristics.

claim: Irbp18, an evolutionarily conserved bZIP gene, heterodimerizes with Xrp1 and with another bZip protein, dATF4.
source: Irbp18, an evolutionarily conserved bZIP gene, heterodimerizes with Xrp1 and with another bZip protein, dATF4.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about Irbp18 protein interactions.

claim: Irbp18 is required for the effects of Xrp1.
source: We show that Irbp18 is required for the effects of Xrp1
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-6.

claim: dATF4 does not share the same phenotype as Xrp1/Irbp18.
source: whereas dATF4 does not share the same phenotype
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Xrp1/Irbp18 is the complex active in Rp mutant cells, independently of other complexes that share Irbp18.
source: indicating that Xrp1/Irbp18 is the complex active in Rp mutant cells, independently of other complexes that share Irbp18.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the differential phenotypes of Irbp18 and dATF4 mutations.

claim: Xrp1 and Irbp18 transcripts and proteins are upregulated in Rp mutant cells by auto-regulatory expression.
source: Xrp1 and Irbp18 transcripts and proteins are upregulated in Rp mutant cells by auto-regulatory expression
evidence: This is supported by protein and mRNA data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Auto-regulatory expression of Xrp1 and Irbp18 depends on the Xrp1 DNA binding domains.
source: that depends on the Xrp1 DNA binding domains
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with domain deletion mutants in Figure 4.

claim: Auto-regulatory expression of Xrp1 and Irbp18 is necessary for cell competition.
source: and is necessary for cell competition
evidence: This is shown by the cell competition phenotypes of domain deletion mutants in Figure 4.

claim: Xrp1 is conserved beyond Drosophila.
source: We show that Xrp1 is conserved beyond Drosophila
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis identifying Xrp1 homologs in other Dipteran insects shown in Figure 8.

claim: Xrp1 is under positive selection for rapid evolution.
source: although under positive selection for rapid evolution
evidence: This is supported by PAML analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: At least one human bZip protein can similarly affect Drosophila development.
source: and that at least one human bZip protein can similarly affect Drosophila development.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments expressing human DDIT3 in Drosophila shown in Figure 8E-G.

claim: Heterozygous Rp+/- animals are viable.
source: Heterozygous Rp+/- animals are viable
evidence: This is established knowledge about Minute mutations cited from prior work (Bridges and Morgan, 1923; Morata and Ripoll, 1975).

claim: Heterozygous Rp+/- animals generally display a slower cell proliferation rate and developmental delay.
source: although they generally display a slower cell proliferation rate and developmental delay (Bridges and Morgan, 1923; Morata and Ripoll, 1975)
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior work.

claim: Rp+/- cells undergo apoptosis when surrounded by wild-type Rp+/+ cells.
source: but Rp+/- cells undergo apoptosis when surrounded by wild-type Rp+/+ cells (Morata and Ripoll, 1975; Simpson and Morata, 1981; Moreno et al., 2002; Li and Baker, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell competition cited from multiple prior studies.

claim: P53 is important for some examples of cell competition in mammals.
source: Interestingly, P53 is important for some examples of cell competition in mammals
evidence: This is cited knowledge from prior work (Baker et al., 2019).

claim: P53 is dispensable for the elimination of Rp+/- cells in Drosophila.
source: but dispensable for the elimination of Rp+/- cells in Drosophila (Baker et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: Xrp1 loss-of-function mutations allow Rp+/- cells to survive when surrounded by wild-type (Rp+/+) cells.
source: Xrp1 loss-of-function mutations allow Rp+/- cells to survive when surrounded by wild-type (Rp+/+) cells, preventing their elimination by cell competition (Baillon et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from prior work and confirmed by data in this study.

claim: Xrp1 is required for the slow growth, reduced translation, and most of the gene expression changes shown by Rp+/- cells.
source: Remarkably, Xrp1 is also required for the slow growth, reduced translation, and most of the gene expression changes shown by Rp+/- cells, showing that Xrp1 is a central mediator of these effects of Rp gene mutations, none of which seems to depend simply on a reduced number of ribosomes (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: Xrp1 encodes a Basic region Leucine-Zipper (bZIP) protein that also has an AT-hook domain.
source: Xrp1 encodes a Basic region Leuzine-Zipper (bZIP) protein that also has an AT-hook domain
evidence: This is established knowledge about Xrp1 protein structure.

claim: Xrp1 was known earlier as a p53-target that is also implicated in P element transposition.
source: and was known earlier as a p53-target that is also implicated in P element transposition (Brodsky et al., 2004; Akdemir et al., 2007; Francis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: Xrp1 has been implicated in coordination of organ growth following local growth retardation.
source: Recently it has also been implicated in coordination of organ growth following local growth retardation (Boulan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from recent prior work.

claim: The bZIP protein encoded by the CG6272 gene was the only heterodimer partner of Xrp1 identified by in vitro FRET assays.
source: The bZIP protein encoded by the CG6272 gene was the only heterodimer partner of Xrp1 identified by in vitro FRET assays (Reinke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: The Xrp1/CG6272 heterodimer is the sequence-specific DNA-binding component of a multiprotein complex that binds to the P-element Terminal Inverted Repeats.
source: This heterodimer is also the sequence-specific DNA-binding component of a multiprotein complex that binds to the P-element Terminal Inverted Repeats leading to the naming of CG6272 as Inverted Repeat Binding Protein 18 (IRBP18) (Francis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: Xrp1 has been described as specific to the genus Drosophila.
source: Unusually, Xrp1 has been described as specific to the genus Drosophila (Akdemir et al., 2007)
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: irbp18 is well-conserved and belongs to the CAAT/Enhancer Binding Protein (C/EBP) superfamily of transcription factors.
source: whereas irbp18 is well-conserved and belongs to the CAAT/Enhancer Binding Protein (C/EBP) superfamily of transcription factors, being most similar to human C/EBPγ (Ramji and Foka, 2002; Francis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: IRBP18 can heterodimerize with dATF4.
source: IRBP18 can also heterodimerize with a second bZIP protein, dATF4 (Reinke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: dATF4, encoded by the cryptocephal (crc) gene, controls molting and metamorphosis as a cofactor for the ecdysone receptor.
source: dATF4, encoded by the cryptocephal (crc) gene, controls molting and metamorphosis as a cofactor for the ecdysone receptor (Gauthier et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: Ecdysone is an important signal for imaginal disc growth.
source: Ecdysone is an important signal for imaginal disc growth (Delanoue et al., 2010; Jaszczak and Halme, 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: dATF4 is neuroprotective in a model of Parkinsons Disease.
source: In addition, dATF4 is neuroprotective in a model of Parkinsons Disease (Celardo et al., 2017)
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: dATF4 regulates 4E-BP transcription downstream of GCN2 during nutrient stress.
source: and regulates 4E-BP transcription downstream of GCN2 during nutrient stress (Kang et al., 2017; Malzer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: dATF4 can heterodimerize with slow border cells (slbo).
source: dATF4 can heterodimerize with a further C/EBP protein, encoded by slow border cells (slbo) (Reinke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: RpL36+/- clones that did not survive in the irbp18+/+ background always survived in the irbp18-/- background.
source: RpL36+/- clones that did not survive in the irbp18+/+ background (B) always survived in the irbp18-/- background (C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: RpS18+/+ cells have a growth and competitive advantage in the irbp18+/+ background and come to dominate wing disc territory, eliminating remaining RpS18+/- cells by cell death.
source: In the irbp18+/+ background (D) these have a growth and competitive advantage and come to dominate wing disc territory, eliminating remaining RpS18+/- cells by cell death (anti-active caspase DCP1 labeling in magenta).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: RpS18+/+ cells had less advantage in the irbp18-/- background.
source: RpS18+/+ cells had less advantage in the irbp18-/- background (E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: RpS18-/- cells survived as small clones in the irbp18-/- background.
source: In addition, reciprocally recombinant RpS18-/- cells survived as small clones (bright green, eg arrows in E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Wing pouch areas were the same in irbp18+/+ and irbp18-/- backgrounds.
source: Wing pouch areas were the same in irbp18+/+ and irbp18-/- backgrounds (p=0.191, two-tailed t-test)
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The RpS18+/+ fractions were not the same in irbp18+/+ and irbp18-/- backgrounds.
source: but the RpS18+/+ fractions were not (p<0.0001, two-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Reciprocal clones of RpS18+/+ irbp18+/+ and RpS18+/+ irbp18-/- cells grew comparably.
source: Reciprocal clones of RpS18+/+ irbp18+/+ and RpS18+/+ irbp18-/- cells grew comparably (G)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Clones of RpS18+/-irbp18-/- cells expanded at the expense of RpS18+/-irbp18+/- cells and RpS18+/-irbp18+/+ cells.
source: whereas clones of RpS18+/-irbp18-/- cells expanded at the expense of RpS18+/-irbp18+/- cells and RpS18+/-irbp18+/+ cells (H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The probability that clone areas are the same in the RpS18+/+ and RpS18+/- backgrounds is 1.4 × 10−9.
source: Probability that clone areas are the same in the RpS18+/+ and RpS18+/- backgrounds = 1.4 × 10−9 (2-tailed t-test with unequal variances).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Whereas Irbp18 had no effect on growth of cells in wild-type wing or eye discs, it reduced the growth and competitiveness of Rp+/- cells.
source: These results indicate that whereas Irbp18 had no effect on growth of cells in wild-type wing or eye discs, it reduced the growth and competitiveness of Rp+/- cells, like Xrp1 does.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Xrp1 knockdown cell-autonomously enhanced growth of RpS18+/- cells.
source: Xrp1 knockdown cell-autonomously enhanced growth of RpS18+/- cells (Figure 2B,E)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 2B,E.

claim: Crc/dATF4 knockdown had the opposite effect to Xrp1 knockdown, severely restricting the growth of RpS18+/- cells.
source: but Crc/dATF4 knockdown had the opposite effect, severely restricting the growth of RpS18+/- cells (Figure 2C,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 2C,E.

claim: The small remaining RpS18+/- dsRNACrc/dATF4 clones were often fragmented, suggesting they were in the process of apoptosis and/or extrusion from the wing disc.
source: The small remaining RpS18+/- dsRNACrc/dATF4 clones were often fragmented, suggesting they were in the process of apoptosis and/or extrusion from the wing disc (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is inferred from the morphology of clones shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Knock down of neither Xrp1 nor dATF4 significantly affected clone size in the wild type (RpS18+/+) background.
source: Knock down of neither Xrp1 nor dATF4 significantly affected clone size in the wild type (RpS18+/+) background (Figure 2F)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Some RpS18+/+ dsRNACrc/dATF4 clones showed signs of fragmentation.
source: although interestingly some RpS18+/+ dsRNACrc/dATF4 clones showed signs of fragmentation (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 2G,H.

claim: Crc/dATF4 had the opposite effects on growth of RpS18+/- cells than did Xrp1 and Irbp18.
source: These findings indicated that Crc/dATF4 had the opposite effects on growth of RpS18+/- cells than did Xrp1 and Irbp18.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Irbp18 protein was elevated in RpS18+/- cells in mosaic wing discs.
source: Indeed, like Xrp1 (Figure 3A,B), Irbp18 protein was elevated in RpS18+/- cells in mosaic wing discs (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Irbp18 upregulation in Rp+/- cells was Xrp1-dependent.
source: We also found that Irbp18 upregulation in Rp+/- cells was Xrp1-dependent, since clones of RpS18+/- Xrp1-/- cells had lower Irbp18 levels (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Clones of RpS18+/- irbp-/- cells failed to upregulate Xrp1 protein.
source: Interestingly, clones of RpS18+/- irbp-/- cells similarly failed to upregulate Xrp1 protein (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: irbp18 transcripts were elevated more than three-fold in non-mosaic RpS3+/- and RpS17+/- wing discs, in an Xrp1-dependent manner.
source: Consistent with these protein findings, mRNA-Seq data (Lee et al., 2018) show irbp18 transcripts elevated more than three-fold in non-mosaic RpS3+/- and RpS17+/- wing discs, in an Xrp1-dependent manner, much as was also seen for Xrp1 mRNA itself (Figure 3I,J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3I,J.

claim: Transcription of a LacZ enhancer trap construct inserted onto the Xrp1 locus was detected upon ectopic expression of Xrp1.
source: Consistent with this, transcription of a LacZ enhancer trap construct inserted onto the Xrp1 locus was detected upon ectopic expression of Xrp1 (Figure 3K,L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 3K,L.

claim: The Xrp1/Irbp18 heterodimer stimulates transcription of Xrp1 and/or irbp18.
source: This cross-regulation between Xrp1 and irbp18 is simply explained if the Xrp1/Irbp18 heterodimer stimulates transcription of Xrp1 and/or irbp18.
evidence: This is inferred from the cross-regulation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The Xrp1attP flox allele behaves as a loss of function allele of Xrp1.
source: The insertion contains an attP sequence and a mini-white gene flanked by LoxP sites. This insertion behaves as a loss of function allele of Xrp1 (Xrp1attP flox; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: The Xrp1attP loxP allele behaves as a wild type allele of Xrp1.
source: Cre-mediated excision of the mini-white gene and other sequences leaves only the attP site and a single LoxP; this allele (Xrp1attP loxP) behaves as a wild type allele of Xrp1 (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: The Xrp1HA allele behaved as a wt allele during cell competition.
source: This Xrp1HA allele behaved as a wt allele during cell competition. That is, RpS18+/- cells were normally outcompeted by wild type cells in the homozygous Xrp1HA background, occupying only the minority of the wing disc and exhibiting competitive cell death at boundaries with RpS18+/+ cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Expression of the Xrp1HA protein was elevated in RpS18+/- cells.
source: As is seen for the endogenous protein, expression of the Xrp1HA protein was elevated in RpS18+/- cells and could be detected with either anti-Xrp1 antibody or with anti-HA (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Alleles encoding Xrp1 proteins lacking either the AT hook or the basic sequence behaved as loss-of-function alleles.
source: In contrast to Xrp1HA, alleles encoding Xrp1 proteins lacking either the AT hook or the basic sequence (Xrp1ΔAT-HA and Xrp1ΔBS-HA, respectively) behaved as loss-of-function alleles, allowing RpS18+/- cells to occupy most of mosaic discs without experiencing competitive cell death (Figure 4E,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 4E,H.

claim: Both Xrp1ΔAT-HA and Xrp1ΔBS-HA prolonged the survival of homozygous RpS18-/- clones.
source: Significantly, both Xrp1ΔAT-HA and Xrp1ΔBS-HA also prolonged the survival of homozygous RpS18-/- clones, which is a feature of Xrp1-/- genotypes (Figure 4E,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 4E,H.

claim: Both Xrp1ΔAT-HA and Xrp1ΔBS-HA impaired the upregulation of Xrp1 in RpS18+/- cells.
source: Both Xrp1ΔAT-HA and Xrp1ΔBS-HA also impaired the upregulation of Xrp1 in RpS18+/- cells, although Xrp1 protein levels were still elevated in RpS18-/- clones (Figure 4F,G,I,J)).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 4F,G,I,J.

claim: DNA-binding domains are essential components of Xrp1 function and auto-regulation in RpS18+/- cells.
source: These results indicate that DNA-binding domains are essential components of Xrp1 function and auto-regulation in RpS18+/- cells.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Xrp1 appears to be elevated in RpS18-/- clones by a mechanism independent of auto-regulation.
source: Xrp1 appears to be elevated in RpS18-/- clones by a mechanism independent of auto-regulation, although Xrp1 function to eliminate RpS18-/- cells still depends on the DNA-binding domains.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Xrp1 is elevated in RpS18-/- clones even when auto-regulation is impaired.

claim: Xrp1 over-expression has a strong effect on cell survival in the normal wing imaginal disc, causing the elimination of Xrp1-expressing cell clones within 72 hr.
source: Xrp1 over-expression has a strong effect on cell survival in the normal wing imaginal disc, causing the elimination of Xrp1-expressing cell clones within 72 hr (Figure 5A–B) (Tsurui-Nishimura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B and cited from prior work.

claim: MARCM clones overexpressing Xrp1 and also homozygous mutant for Irbp18 survived, proliferated and were present in the wing epithelium 72 hr after clone induction.
source: By contrast, MARCM clones overexpressing Xrp1 and also homozygous mutant for Irbp18 (CG6272f05006) survived, proliferated and were present in the wing epithelium 72 hr after clone induction (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The negative effect of Xrp1 on growth and survival of wing disc clones depended on Irbp18.
source: Therefore the negative effect of Xrp1 on growth and survival of wing disc clones depended on Irbp18.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Ectopic expression of Irbp18 had no effect on clone survival.
source: In contrast to Xrp1, ectopic expression of Irbp18 had no effect on clone survival (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Ectopic expression of Xrp1 using the GMR-gal4 driver at 18°C leads to a small, glossy eye.
source: During eye development, ectopic expression of Xrp1 using the GMR-gal4 driver at 18°C, leads to a small, glossy eye (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The eye phenotype of ectopic Xrp1 was almost completely suppressed in the absence of irbp18.
source: Like the effect on Xrp1 in the wing, the eye phenotype of ectopic Xrp1 was almost completely suppressed in the absence of irbp18, so that irbp18-/- GMR >Xrp1 eyes were close to wild type in size (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: At 25°C, GMR > Xrp1 reduces the eye to only a small remnant.
source: At 25°C, GMR > Xrp1 reduces the eye to only a small remnant (Figure 6C) (Tsurui-Nishimura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6C and cited from prior work.

claim: At 25°C, eye size was rescued considerably in the Irbp18 mutant background, but the eyes were not normal, instead having a glossy appearance.
source: Although eye size was rescued considerably in the Irbp18 mutant background, the eyes were not normal, instead having a glossy appearance (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The glossy eye phenotype at 25°C was definitely due to ectopic Xrp1.
source: This phenotype was definitely due to ectopic Xrp1, because both eye size and appearance were rescued by co-expressing dsRNA for Xrp1 along with ectopic Xrp1 (dsRNA for Xrp1 had no effect on eye development by itself)(Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The restoration of eye size definitely reflected a requirement for Irbp18.
source: The restoration of eye size definitely reflected a requirement for Irbp18, because a less complete rescue was seen when co-expressing dsRNA for Irbp18 (Figure 6F), and because restoring Irbp18 expression to the Irbp18 mutant restored the full GMR > Xrp1 size reduction (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6F,G.

claim: Xrp1 function at higher temperature remains substantially dependent on Irbp18 but also exhibited an Irbp18-independent component.
source: Therefore, Xrp1 function at higher temperature remains substantially dependent on Irbp18 but also exhibited an Irbp18-independent component.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Ectopic expression of Irbp18 had no effect on the eye.
source: Ectopic expression of Irbp18 had no effect on the eye (Figure 6H)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: GMR-gal4 drove strong expression of Irbp18 in the eye imaginal disc.
source: although we confirmed by in situ hybridization that GMR-gal4 drove strong expression in the eye imaginal disc (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The eye imaginal disc from GMR > Xrp1 exhibited apoptosis soon after Xrp1 was expressed.
source: The eye imaginal disc from GMR > Xrp1 exhibited apoptosis soon after Xrp1 was expressed (Figure 6J,K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6J,K.

claim: Apoptosis in GMR > Xrp1 eye discs was dependent on irbp18.
source: This apoptosis was dependent on irbp18 (Figure 6L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6L.

claim: Cell divisions are reduced in GMR > Xrp1 eye imaginal discs.
source: This eye disc region overlaps the second mitotic wave of dividing cells, and cell divisions are reduced in GMR > Xrp1 eye imaginal discs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-D) (Tsurui-Nishimura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-D and cited from prior work.

claim: Co-overexpression of either anti-apoptotic proteins P35 or diap1 only rescued the GMR > Xrp1 eye phenotype modestly.
source: Co-overexpression of either anti-apoptotic proteins P35 or diap1 (Figure 6M,N), or depletion of caspases and pro-apoptotic proteins only rescued the GMR > Xrp1 eye phenotype modestly (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E-J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6M,N and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E-J.

claim: Over-expression of UAS-Rheb enlarged wild type eyes.
source: Whereas over-expression of UAS-Rheb enlarged wild type eyes (Figure 6O)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6O.

claim: Over-expression of UAS-Rheb had no effect on GMR-Xrp1 eyes.
source: it had no effect on GMR-Xrp1 eyes (Figure 6P).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6P.

claim: Over-expression of UAS-yki enlarged wild type eyes.
source: By contrast over-expression of UAS-yki both enlarged wild type eyes (Figure 6Q)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6Q.

claim: Over-expression of UAS-yki partially rescued the GMR > Xrp1 eye phenotype.
source: and partially rescued the GMR > Xrp1 eye phenotype (Figure 6R).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6R.

claim: Co-expression of Yki was able to rescue the viability of wild-type MARCM clones overexpressing Xrp1 in the wing imaginal disc.
source: Co-expression of Yki was also able to rescue the viability of wild-type MARCM clones overexpressing Xrp1 in the wing imaginal disc (Figure 6S,T).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6S,T.

claim: Ectopic Xrp1 affects proliferation and survival.
source: Thus, as noted previously (Akdemir et al., 2007; Tsurui-Nishimura et al., 2013), ectopic Xrp1 affects proliferation and survival
evidence: This is cited from prior work and confirmed by data in this study.

claim: Yki is able to modulate the effects of ectopic Xrp1.
source: but Yki is able to modulate the effects.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Deleting the C-terminal region of Xrp1 abolished function.
source: while deleting the C-terminal region of Xrp1 abolished function (Figure 7M–P)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 7M-P.

claim: Deletion of each individual domain (AT-hook, basic region, or Leucine Zipper) reduced Xrp1 function but did not eliminate it.
source: deletion of each individual domain reduced function but did not eliminate it (Figure 7Q–X).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 7Q-X.

claim: The C-terminal portion of the Xrp1 protein is necessary overall.
source: These data indicate that the C-terminal portion of the Xrp1 protein is necessary overall
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Each of the LZ, BR and AT domains contributes to Xrp1 function, even when Xrp1 transcription is under Gal4/UAS control.
source: and each of the LZ, BR and AT domains contributes to Xrp1 function, even when Xrp1 transcription is under Gal4/UAS control.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: There is evidence of diversification under positive selection in 13 Drosophila species, with 68 amino acid positions changing rapidly in Xrp1.
source: We discovered evidence of diversification under positive selection in these 13 species, with 68 amino acid positions changing rapidly in Xrp1 (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PAML analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Xrp1 was under strong positive selection for evolutionary change.
source: This result suggested that Xrp1 was under strong positive selection for evolutionary change.
evidence: This is inferred from the PAML analysis results.

claim: Divergent Xrp1 homologs exist in other Dipteran insects.
source: Using BLAST searches we have now identified apparent Xrp1 orthologs in other Dipteran insects (Figure 8B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: All Xrp1 homologs share the AT-hook and bZIP domains.
source: All share the AT-hook and bZIP domains (Figure 8C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence alignment shown in Figure 8C.

claim: All Xrp1 homologs share a separated Xrp1-homology domain more amino-terminal in the protein, which is the most highly conserved region of Xrp1.
source: and a separated Xrp1-homology domain more amino-terminal in the protein, which is in fact the most highly conserved region of Xrp1 (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence alignment shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Outside of the conserved domains, the Xrp1 proteins appear to be highly divergent.
source: Outside of these domains, the Xrp1 proteins appear to be highly divergent (Figure 8B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1 ).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: DDIT3 encodes a protein that shares some properties with Xrp1.
source: The DNA Damage Induced Transcript 3 (DDIT3) encodes a protein that shares some properties with Xrp1.
evidence: This is based on comparison of known properties of DDIT3 and Xrp1.

claim: Like Xrp1, DDIT3 is induced in response to DNA damage.
source: Like Xrp1, DDIT3 is induced in response to DNA damage
evidence: This is established knowledge about DDIT3.

claim: Like Xrp1, DDIT3 regulates apoptosis.
source: regulates apoptosis
evidence: This is established knowledge about DDIT3.

claim: Like Xrp1, DDIT3 heterodimerizes with C/EBPγ.
source: and heterodimerizes with C/EBPγ.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DDIT3.

claim: DDIT3 lacks any recognizable ortholog in Drosophila.
source: DDIT3, also known as CHOP, lacks any recognizable ortholog in Drosophila.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: Phylogenetic bootstrapping analysis has suggested that DDIT3 might be the most similar human bZip domain to that of Drosophila Xrp1.
source: Interestingly, phylogenetic bootstrapping analysis has suggested that DDIT3 might be the most similar human bZip domain to that of Drosophila Xrp1 (Baillon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: Ectopic expression of hDDIT3 reduced eye size in Drosophila.
source: Interestingly, the ectopic expression of hDDIT3 not only reduced the eye size like Xrp1 does (Figure 8E)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The eye phenotype of ectopic hDDIT3 was ameliorated by the simultaneous expression of RNAi against Irbp18.
source: but this phenotype was ameliorated by the simultaneous expression of RNAi against Irbp18 (Figure 8F)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The eye phenotype of ectopic hDDIT3 was ameliorated by the simultaneous expression of RNAi against Xrp1.
source: or Xrp1 (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Xrp1 and irbp18 are both necessary for the slow-growth and cell competition of Rp+/- cells.
source: Our results show that Xrp1 and irbp18 are both necessary for the slow-growth and cell competition of Rp+/- cells
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Xrp1 and irbp18 act apparently independently of other IRBP18 partners.
source: apparently independently of other IRBP18 partners
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the differential phenotypes of Irbp18 and dATF4 mutations.

claim: The upregulation of both Xrp1 and irbp18 in Rp+/- cells depends on one another's function.
source: Additionally, we find that the upregulation of both Xrp1 and irbp18 in Rp+/- cells depends on one another's function
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The DNA binding and dimerization domains are important for the function and regulation of Xrp1 and irbp18.
source: and that the DNA binding and dimerization domains are important for the function and regulation of these genes
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 7.

claim: There is an auto-regulatory loop based on the Xrp1/IRBP18 heterodimer that is necessary for cell competition.
source: further evidence of an auto-regulatory loop based on the Xrp1/IRBP18 heterodimer and necessary for cell competition.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data on auto-regulation and domain requirements.

claim: Divergent mammalian proteins might resemble Xrp1 functionally.
source: Finally, we identify rapidly-evolving Xrp1 homologs beyond Drosophila and suggest that divergent mammalian proteins might resemble Xrp1 functionally.
evidence: This is suggested based on the functional similarity of hDDIT3 to Xrp1 in Drosophila.

claim: The Xrp1/Irbp18 and Crc/IRBP18 heterodimers have independent and perhaps unrelated functions.
source: Taken together, our findings suggest that the Xrp1/IRBP18 and Crc/IRBP18 heterodimers have independent and perhaps unrelated functions.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the differential phenotypes of Irbp18 and dATF4 mutations.

claim: IRBP18 is normally made in excess.
source: Consistent with this, ectopic expression of IRBP18 had no phenotypic effect, suggesting that IRBP18 is normally made in excess
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of phenotype upon IRBP18 overexpression.

claim: Xrp1 is limiting for the growth inhibiting activities of the Xrp1/IRBP18 heterodimers.
source: so that it is Xrp1 that is limiting for the growth inhibiting activities of the Xrp1/IRBP18 heterodimers
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of phenotype upon IRBP18 overexpression.

claim: The Xrp1/IRBP18 heterodimers do not impact IRBP18 availability sufficiently to affect Crc/Irbp18 functions.
source: which do not impact IRBP18 availability sufficiently to affect Crc/Irbp18 functions.
evidence: This is inferred from the independent functions of the two heterodimers.

claim: The basic and Leucine Zipper domains were important for Xrp1 function.
source: As expected if Xrp1 functions in a heterodimer, the basic and Leucine Zipper domains were important for Xrp1 function, as was the AT hook.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 7.

claim: In over-expression assays, there could be reduced activity of proteins deleted for any of the AT-hook, basic, or Leucine Zipper domains individually, but not of a truncation that precedes them all.
source: In over-expression assays only, there could be reduced activity of proteins deleted for any of these domains individually, but not of a truncation that precedes them all.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: When encoded from the endogenous locus, basic and AT-hook domains appeared absolutely required.
source: When encoded from the endogenous locus, basic and AT-hook domains appeared absolutely required.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mutual auto-regulation may be a significant feature of Xrp1 and IRBP18 function.
source: Mutual auto-regulation may be a significant feature of Xrp1 and IRBP18 function.
evidence: This is inferred from the cross-regulation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The elevated Xrp1 and irbp18 transcription observed in Rp+/- wing discs is dependent on Xrp1 function.
source: As noted previously, the elevated Xrp1 and irbp18 transcription observed in Rp+/- wing discs is dependent on Xrp1 function (Baillon et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2018)(Figure 3Q–R).
evidence: This is cited from prior work and confirmed by data in this study.

claim: irbp18 is required for the autoregulation of Xrp1.
source: Here we show that IRBP18 protein levels are also elevated in Rp+/- cells in an Xrp1-dependent fashion, and that irbp18 is also required for the autoregulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Xrp1 was still substantially dependent on the irbp18 gene and on the Leucine Zipper and DNA binding domains when expressed using GAL4-driven transgenes.
source: This cannot be completely correct, however, because Xrp1 was still substantially dependent on the irbp18 gene and on the Leucine Zipper and DNA binding domains when expressed using GAL4-driven transgenes that are independent of auto-regulation
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figures 5-7.

claim: By-passing the requirement of auto-regulation does not relieve the requirements for heterodimerization and DNA binding domains.
source: so by-passing the requirement of auto-regulation does not relieve the requirements for heterodimerization and DNA binding domains.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data on ectopic expression.

claim: Xrp1 and irbp18 are both required to promptly eliminate Rp-/- cells, where their expression does not require auto-regulation.
source: It is also worth noting that Xrp1 and irbp18 are both required to promptly eliminate Rp-/- cells, where their expression does not require auto-regulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data showing survival of Rp-/- cells in Xrp1 and irbp18 mutants.

claim: There are other transcriptional targets of Xrp1/IRBP18 in Rp+/- and Rp-/- cells besides Xrp1 and irbp18 themselves.
source: Although implicating other transcriptional targets of Xrp1/IRBP18 in Rp+/- and Rp-/- cells, these studies do not rule out other functions besides transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for DNA binding domains even when auto-regulation is bypassed.

claim: Xrp1 genes have been under strong positive selection for rapid evolutionary change.
source: We found, however, that Xrp1 genes have been under strong positive selection for rapid evolutionary change.
evidence: This is demonstrated by PAML analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Recurrent positive selection is often the sign of an evolutionary arms race.
source: Recurrent positive selection is often the sign of an evolutionary arms race, such as are often driven by host-pathogen interactions, sexual competition, or intra-genomic conflict (Valen, 1973; Sawyer et al. (2005); Clark et al. (2006); Elde and Malik (2009); Levine and Malik (2013); Enard et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about evolutionary biology cited from prior work.

claim: Pathogens might target Xrp1 to promote growth and survival of infected cells.
source: Possibly pathogens target Xrp1 to promote growth and survival of infected cells.
evidence: This is speculation about the reason for positive selection on Xrp1.

claim: Xrp1 is documented to interact with the P element transposable element.
source: It is interesting that Xrp1 is already documented to interact with one transposable element, the P element (Francis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: Rapid divergence makes homology difficult to detect.
source: Rapid divergence makes homology difficult to detect
evidence: This is established knowledge about evolutionary biology.

claim: Divergent Xrp1 homologs in other Dipteran insects have not previously been annotated because their sequence similarities are restricted to the key DNA-binding portion of the protein, and to a more amino-terminal Xrp1-homology domain.
source: and accordingly we now identify divergent Xrp1 homologs in other Dipteran insects that have not previously been annotated because their sequence similarities are restricted to the key DNA-binding portion of the protein, and to a more amino-terminal Xrp1-homology domain.
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: The failure to identify more distant Xrp1 homologs might be genuine, or might reflect further divergence beyond our ability to recognize homology.
source: The failure to identify still more distant homologs might be genuine, or might reflect further divergence beyond our ability to recognize homology.
evidence: This is speculation about the limits of sequence analysis.

claim: Mammals contain other members of the C/EBP protein family without identified Drosophila homologs.
source: Mammals do contain other members of the C/EBP protein family without identified Drosophila homologs
evidence: This is established knowledge about C/EBP proteins.

claim: DDIT3 can generate a similar phenotype to Xrp1 when expressed in Drosophila.
source: and we show that DDIT3 (aka CHOP and C/EBP-Z) can generate a similar phenotype to Xrp1 when expressed in Drosophila.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 8E-G.

claim: C/EBP-α has been implicated in a cell competition-like phenomenon, the elimination of cells from the multipotent hematopoietic stem cell niche following irradiation.
source: Interestingly C/EBP-α, one of the mammalian proteins more related to Irbp18, has been implicated in a cell competition-like phenomenon, the elimination of cells from the multipotent hematopoietic stem cell niche following irradiation (Fleenor et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.
